messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 46-year-old curriculum designer who grew up in a small Midwestern city and now lives with his wife and two teenagers in a quiet suburb. He was pulled over late one winter evening three years ago on his way home from a late meeting. The officer claimed Kwame had failed to signal a lane change, but within moments the encounter escalated: Kwame was ordered out of the car, forced to the ground, and held at gunpoint while another officer searched his vehicle. For several minutes, lying face-down on the cold asphalt, he felt the full weight of a knee pressing into his back and heard the officers shouting commands he could not process. He could not speak. The search yielded nothing, and he was eventually told he could leave—no citation, no apology. Kwame drove home in stunned silence, his hands still trembling on the wheel.

In the weeks that followed, he tried to convince himself it was just a bad stop, something to put behind him. But the world felt different. He began to notice how often he scanned parking lots for patrol cars, how his shoulders tightened whenever a police cruiser appeared in his rearview mirror. At work, in his quiet office where he designs lesson plans and district curricula, a sudden knock on the door made him flinch. His wife noticed he no longer liked driving after dark, and that he would go out of his way to avoid the intersection where it happened. Kwame himself attributed this to simple caution. But the physical reactions were harder to dismiss: his heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that left him shaky for minutes afterward.

These moments of heightened threat—the sudden siren on the highway, a uniformed officer in a coffee shop—did not just pass. Increasingly, they brought with them a wave of emotion that felt exactly as overwhelming as the night itself, yet without any clear image or story attached. Kwame would feel the terror pressing in, the same suffocating helplessness, but if someone asked him what he was thinking, he could not say. He could not put the event into words; the memory existed only as a visceral weight in his chest. Sometimes, in the middle of a calm evening at home, he would feel the full intensity of that night descend on him from nowhere—no police car, no sound—just the raw emotion, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing, sit very still, and wait for it to pass. His wife once asked what was wrong, and he could only shake his head, unable to form a sentence.

Over time, a pattern took hold. A trigger—the reflection of a patrol car in a storefront, the rhythm of a police helicopter overhead—would set off a startle, a physical reaction that immediately flooded him with the unspeakable, imageless memory. The more hypervigilant he became, the more often the threat cues appeared, and the more frequently he was hit by that overwhelming, wordless recall. He began to feel like he was always bracing for the next wave, scanning his environment even in the safety of his own home. At work, he volunteered to handle projects that required no outside meetings, no unexpected interactions. He stopped going to the gym because the locker room door could be slammed shut, sending him into a panic.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was an incident at a school district event. A local police officer had been invited to talk about community safety, and Kwame, cornered by his supervisor into attending, found himself unable to breathe when the officer walked into the room. He excused himself to the restroom, where he stood gripping the sink, his chest heaving, unable to shake the feeling that he was back on the ground. His supervisor found him and asked if he was okay. Kwame said yes, but he could not stop shaking. That night, he told his wife everything—not the details, because he still could not find words for them, but the fear, the avoidance, the way his own body had become a minefield. She made the appointment. As he sits in the clinician’s office, Kwame is terrified that revisiting the memory will undo him completely, but he is also exhausted from a life lived on constant guard, waiting for the next moment his own body will betray him with the past.
